title: MMRDA signs Surbana Jurong to master-plan Mumbai 3.0
summary: A Singapore planner will draw the vision and master plan for a new city across 124 villages in Raigad.
points: Spread across about 323.44 sq km and 124 villages
Covers Panvel, Uran and Pen talukas of Raigad district
Integrates land use, mobility and infrastructure plans
Built around transit-oriented, mixed-use development
body: The Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA) has signed an agreement with Singapore-headquartered Surbana Jurong Infrastructure Pte. Ltd. to prepare the Vision Document, Master Plan and related planning framework for Mumbai 3.0. It is a major step towards turning Maharashtra's vision for a new global urban and economic growth centre into a structured plan.

The agreement was signed by Dr. Sanjay Mukherjee, IAS, Metropolitan Commissioner, MMRDA, and Mr. Avinash Mishra, Chief Executive, South Asia, Surbana Jurong, in the presence of Chief Minister of Maharashtra Shri Devendra Fadnavis. Surbana Jurong's roots are closely linked with Singapore's own transformation into a model of planned urbanisation, housing and industrial development.
Mumbai 3.0 is spread across approximately 323.44 sq km, covering 124 villages across Panvel, Uran and Pen talukas of Raigad district.

Surbana Jurong will prepare an Inception Plan, Existing Situation Analysis, Vision Plan, Draft Concept Land Use Plan, stakeholder consultations and a Final Concept Plan. The work will study existing land use, roads and mobility, demographics, socio-economic conditions, utilities, environmental features and public amenities before setting the long-term spatial and economic framework for the new city.

The Vision Document will define Mumbai 3.0's economic positioning, growth strategy, investment themes, catalytic projects and place-making principles. It will also draw on global best practice in integrated urban development, smart infrastructure, mixed-use districts, public spaces, renewable energy, digital infrastructure, Transit-Oriented Development and innovation-led economies.

The Draft Concept Plan brings together three parts: a Concept Structure Plan (land-use patterns, development nodes and growth corridors), a Concept Mobility Plan (regional and intra-city connectivity, mass transit, multimodal and pedestrian movement, and Transit-Oriented Development) and a Concept Infrastructure Plan (water supply, sewerage, storm-water drainage, solid waste, power, gas, social infrastructure and blue-green networks).

title: Mumbai property registrations hit a 14-year August high
summary: 12,401 registrations, up 11% year-on-year, with both primary and secondary housing on the rise.
points: 12,401 property registrations recorded in August
Up 11 percent year-on-year
The highest August figure in 14 years
Growth seen in both primary and secondary housing
body: Property registrations in Mumbai rose 11 percent year-on-year, with the city recording 12,401 registrations by 5:20 pm on a Monday. It is the highest August figure in 14 years and points to a rise in both primary and secondary housing.

title: India REITs: gaining scale and unlocking value
summary: Listed REITs and InvITs now hold over 195 million sq ft, with about 37 million sq ft more in the pipeline.
points: Existing REIT/InvIT portfolio has passed 195 million sq ft
About 37 million sq ft upcoming, as of March 2026
Office holds around 84% of the operational portfolio
Retail, industrial and warehousing are gaining momentum
body: Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) are speeding up the institutionalisation and democratisation of India's real estate sector. Rising investor participation, strong performance of the underlying assets, asset acquisitions and supportive policies are all driving the shift.

The REIT/InvIT ecosystem has grown steadily over the past five to six years in asset class and size, geography and investor base. The market now has five office-focused REITs, a retail REIT and an industrial and warehousing InvIT, showing how well these structures scale in India.

According to Colliers' report "India REITs: Gaining scale & unlocking value", the portfolio across listed REITs and InvITs has passed 195 million sq ft, with an upcoming pipeline of about 37 million sq ft as of March 2026. Office still dominates with around 84% of the operational portfolio, while retail and industrial and warehousing are gaining momentum.

title: India's real estate set for a 20X leap by 2047
summary: From under USD 1 trillion today to a USD 5–10 trillion market, opening new urban growth corridors.
points: Under USD 1 trillion today, USD 5–10 trillion by 2047
Could contribute 14–20% of India's GDP
New urban growth corridors are opening up
Aligned with the Viksit Bharat vision for Amrit Kaal
body: India's real estate sector is set for a 20X leap by 2047, unlocking new urban growth corridors and potentially becoming a USD 5–10 trillion market.

The market is on course to grow from under USD 1 trillion today to USD 5–10 trillion by 2047, potentially contributing 14–20% of the country's GDP. The transformation tracks India's broader economic rise and shapes the vision of Viksit Bharat under the Amrit Kaal roadmap.

title: Mumbai redevelopment: 910 societies, 326.8 acres unlocked
summary: Society redevelopment has grown from a handful of deals in 2020 into a structured, scalable market.
points: 910 society redevelopment agreements from 2020 to H1 2025
Over 326.8 acres (1.3 mn sq m) of land unlocked for renewal
One of the largest land recycling waves post-DCPR 2034
Every agreement is registered with the IGR
body: Mumbai's redevelopment momentum has changed a great deal in recent years. From a nascent phase with limited deal activity in 2020, the market has become a far more structured and scalable ecosystem.

Between 2020 and H1 2025, 910 society-level redevelopment agreements were recorded, together unlocking over 326.8 acres (1.3 mn sq m) of potential land for renewal. It is one of the largest land recycling waves the city has seen in the post-DCPR 2034 era.

Development Agreements (DAs) are the legal contracts between a housing society and a developer. They set out obligations for rehabilitation, free-sale area, timelines and financial commitments. DAs must be registered with the Inspector General of Registration (IGR), the state authority, which creates an official record of redevelopment activity.

title: How DCPR 2034 is powering Mumbai's redevelopment
summary: FSI incentives and zone-specific rules have turned regulation into a redevelopment engine.
points: Incentive FSI for tenant rehousing or public benefit
Cluster schemes get amalgamation bonuses and relaxed norms
33(9) cluster redevelopment allows up to 4.0 FSI or more
33(7B) opens redevelopment to standalone societies
body: Mumbai's redevelopment surge is not a spontaneous market outcome. It comes from a purpose-built policy ecosystem shaped to tackle the city's twin problems of land scarcity and ageing housing stock. Over the last decade, regulation has moved from fragmented controls to an integrated framework built around FSI incentives, financial instruments and zone-specific levers.

The Development Control and Promotion Regulations (DCPR) 2034 replaced DCR 1991 and fundamentally redefined how land, density and incentives work in Mumbai. Its key enablers include incentive FSI for projects with tenant rehousing obligations or public benefit, and higher buildability for cluster and composite redevelopment through amalgamation bonuses and relaxed design norms.
Cessed buildings under 33(7): covers cessed (pre-1969) buildings in the Island City, with FSI linked to Table 30(A) and a 50% incentive over the rehab requirement.
Cluster redevelopment under 33(9): designed for larger land tracts, typically over 4,000–6,000 sq m, allowing up to 4.0 FSI or higher in special incentive zones.
Independent societies under 33(7B): enables redevelopment of standalone societies, especially relevant in the suburbs, with FSI adjusted for road width and plot conditions.
MHADA buildings under 33(5): applies to MHADA layouts, often with low-income or rental housing, allowing up to 4.0 FSI plus further incentives depending on tenant count and amenities.

source.name: Knight Frank, Upgrading Mumbai: The Redevelopment Story 2025

title: MHADA lottery 2026: 2,640 Mumbai homes drawn, and what winners do next
summary: MHADA's Mumbai Board drew 2,640 homes from 97,000+ applications. Here is how winners claim theirs.
points: 2,640 homes: 145 EWS, 858 LIG, 1,408 MIG and 229 HIG
More than 97,000 applications, over 75,300 valid EMD payers
Winners verify documents, then pay the balance on time
Late payment can lead to the allotment being cancelled
body: The Mumbai Board of the Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority (MHADA) held its computerised lottery for 2,640 homes on 6 August 2026 at 12 pm. It received more than 97,000 applications, of which over 75,300 applicants had paid a valid earnest money deposit (EMD).

The homes are spread across four income groups: 145 for the Economically Weaker Section (EWS), 858 for the Low Income Group (LIG), 1,408 for the Middle Income Group (MIG) and 229 for the High Income Group (HIG). The income limits are up to Rs 6 lakh a year for EWS, Rs 6 to 9 lakh for LIG, Rs 9 to 12 lakh for MIG and above Rs 12 lakh for HIG.

Winners first download their Provisional Offer Letter or Intimation Letter from their MHADA account or the mobile app. They then submit their documents for verification at the designated MHADA office, including identity, address and income proof, along with any other papers named in the offer letter.

The remaining amount must be paid within the timeline MHADA sets, and late payment may lead to the allotment being cancelled. Advisory firm Propserve, quoted in the report, puts this at the remaining 90% of the home's value within 60 to 90 days, so it suggests winners line up home-loan approval early. Once documents and payment are cleared, MHADA completes the allotment and registration and possession follow.

Buyers should also budget for registration costs: stamp duty of 5% of the property value for men and 4% for women, plus a registration fee of 1% capped at Rs 30,000 for most residential properties. GST, society maintenance and other statutory charges apply where relevant.
MHADA homes are generally priced below regular market rates. Propserve estimates that its HIG homes come roughly 20% to 30% below comparable private projects.
